note: These notes compare how two people described themselves. They are conversation starters, not predictions: no pattern of scores makes a relationship more or less likely to work.

poles.higher: enjoy new ideas, variety and trying things a different way
poles.lower: prefer familiar, practical and proven ways of doing things

shared.higher: You may both chase new ideas and plans. Check that someone also keeps track of what is already working.
shared.middle: You can probably meet each other halfway between new ideas and familiar routines.
shared.lower: You may both prefer the familiar. Now and then, choose something new to try together on purpose.

openness.complement: One of you can bring fresh options while the other keeps plans grounded and realistic.
openness.misunderstanding: Suggestions for change can feel unsettling to one of you, while sticking with the usual can feel dull to the other.
openness.prompt: When did one of you suggest something new recently? How did each of you feel about it?

poles.higher: like plans, order and finishing things early
poles.lower: like flexibility, spontaneity and deciding closer to the time

shared.higher: You may both like plans and standards. Agree where "good enough" is fine, so neither of you carries all the pressure.
shared.middle: You can probably agree on a level of planning that suits you both.
shared.lower: You may both prefer to keep things open. Agree on the few deadlines and tasks that really need a plan.

conscientiousness.complement: One of you can keep shared tasks on track while the other keeps room for flexibility and fun.
conscientiousness.misunderstanding: Reminders and plans can feel like pressure to one of you, while a relaxed approach can feel careless to the other.
conscientiousness.prompt: Which shared task or plan causes the most friction? What would each of you need to feel comfortable with it?

poles.higher: recharge through company and like to talk things through
poles.lower: recharge through quiet time and like to think before speaking

shared.higher: You may both enjoy busy, social plans. Check in now and then about whether either of you needs a quieter stretch.
shared.middle: You can probably balance social time and quiet time without much negotiation.
shared.lower: You may both enjoy quiet time. Make sure important topics still get talked about out loud.

extraversion.complement: One of you can open up conversations and social plans while the other brings calm and careful listening.
extraversion.misunderstanding: Needing time alone can look like withdrawal to one of you, while wanting to talk straight away can feel like pressure to the other.
extraversion.prompt: After a long day, what does each of you need first: conversation, or some quiet? How could you make room for both?

poles.higher: put harmony first and adapt to keep things smooth
poles.lower: say what they think directly, even if it causes some friction

shared.higher: You may both avoid disagreement. Make it safe to raise small concerns before they grow.
shared.middle: You can probably mix warmth and honesty in a way that feels fair to you both.
shared.lower: You may both be direct. Remember to say what you appreciate as well as what you disagree with.

agreeableness.complement: One of you can keep conversations warm while the other makes sure hard topics are named.
agreeableness.misunderstanding: Directness can feel harsh to one of you, while going along with things can feel unclear or unspoken to the other.
agreeableness.prompt: Think of a recent disagreement. What did each of you want the other to understand?

poles.higher: stay calm under pressure and recover quickly from setbacks
poles.lower: feel worry and stress strongly and notice what might go wrong

shared.higher: You may both stay calm under pressure. Check that worries still get a chance to be heard.
shared.middle: You can probably support each other through ordinary ups and downs.
shared.lower: You may both feel stress strongly. Agree on small ways to slow down and support each other on hard days.

emotional_stability.complement: One of you can bring steadiness while the other notices risks early and cares about getting things right.
emotional_stability.misunderstanding: Calm can look like not caring to one of you, while worry can look like overreacting to the other.
emotional_stability.prompt: When one of you is stressed, what helps, and what doesn't? Be specific.

exercises.title: Two-minute turns
steps: Pick one topic that matters to you both.
One person talks for two minutes while the other only listens.
The listener sums up what they heard, then you swap.

exercises.title: Needs, not labels
steps: Each of you finishes the sentence "When I'm stressed, it helps me when you…".
Swap answers and ask one question each.
Agree on one small thing to try this week.

exercises.title: Strengths swap
steps: Each of you names one way the other's style has helped you.
Name one situation where your styles clash.
Decide who takes the lead in that situation next time.

shared_goals: Have one unhurried conversation each week about how things are going.
Agree on one shared plan and how much detail it needs.
Ask before giving advice: "Do you want ideas, or just someone to listen?"
